topics.title: Ken-Betwa Project
bullets: On 19 July 2026, MP Police cleared a 15-day Ken-Betwa protest at Kupi village, detaining leader Amit Bhatnagar (on hunger strike for 14 days) and 150 protesters.
Bhatnagar was hospitalised due to deteriorating health; protesters staged 'jal satyagraha', 'chita satyagraha' and symbolic 'faansi satyagraha' .
The protest highlighted grievances over land acquisition, rehabilitation, compensation irregularities, and environmental concerns Background –
The Ken-Betwa Link Project (KBLP) is India's first river interlinking project under the National Perspective Plan (NPP).
It aims to transfer surplus water from the Ken river to the Betwa basin through the Daudhan Dam and a 221-km canal.
The project will provide irrigation, drinking water, and hydropower across Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh.
The Union Cabinet cleared the project in December 2021 at an estimated cost of ₹44,605 crore .
The foundation stone was laid in December 2024.
The project will submerge 6,017 hectares of forest, affect 7,193 families, and provide irrigation to 10 lakh hectares and drinking water to 62 lakh people. About the Project –
The project aims to provide irrigation to more than 10 lakh hectares of farmland in the drought-prone Bundelkhand region.
It will provide drinking water to approximately 62 lakh people and generate hydroelectric power.
The government has described the project as a major development initiative to address water shortages and boost economic growth in the region.
The project involves the construction of a 77-metre-high Daudhan Dam on the Ken river in Chhatarpur district, Madhya Pradesh .
The link canal will have a length of 221 km, including a 2 km tunnel .
Two power projects have also been proposed as part of the project .
Under the displacement policy, affected families are entitled to ₹12.5 lakh per adult as compensation.
If a person opts for a plot, ₹5 lakh will be deducted from the compensation, and the remaining ₹7.5 lakh will be given in cash.
The state government has sanctioned an additional ₹202.5 crore for rehabilitation, increasing assistance from ₹5 lakh to ₹12.5 lakh per eligible family.
The project will affect approximately 6,017 hectares of forest area in and around the Panna Tiger Reserve (PTR).
Around 17,101 trees have been identified for felling, of which 12,404 trees have already been felled within the Panna Tiger Reserve.
The project will also impact the Ken Gharial Sanctuary and submerge nearly 98 sq km of the tiger reserve.
An Integrated Landscape Management Plan (ILMP) has been prepared by the Wildlife Institute of India (WII) to mitigate the environmental impact .
The ILMP aims to improve habitat quality, maintain critical wildlife corridors linking adjacent Protected Areas, and protect flagship species – including tigers, vultures, and gharials .
A Greater Panna Landscape Council (GPLC) has been constituted under the chairmanship of the Chief Secretary of Madhya Pradesh to ensure systematic implementation of the ILMP .
A Central Empowered Committee (CEC) was constituted by the Supreme Court to examine the wildlife clearance for the project.
The CEC raised concerns about the project's impact on the ecological integrity of Panna Tiger Reserve and recommended studies on mitigative measures.

The Forest Advisory Committee (FAC) and environmental experts have warned that the project will involve felling of approx. 46 lakh trees (each with a girth greater than 20 cm) from the forest area alone. National Perspective Plan –
The NPP was formulated in 1980 by the Ministry of Irrigation (now Jal Shakti) for inter-basin transfer of water from surplus to deficit basins.
It aims to mitigate floods and droughts by diverting flood water to water-short regions and recharging groundwater.
The National Water Development Agency (NWDA), set up in 1982, is responsible for implementing the ILR programme under the NPP.
The NPP comprises 30 identified interlinking projects: 16 under the Peninsular Component and 14 under the Himalayan Component.
Peninsular Component includes links like Ken-Betwa, Godavari-Krishna, and Krishna-Pennar.
Himalayan Component includes projects like Kosi-Ghaghra, Gandak-Ganga, and Ghaghra-Yamuna.
Pre-Feasibility Reports (PFRs) have been completed for all 30 projects.
Feasibility Reports (FRs) have been finalised for 26 projects.
Detailed Project Reports (DPRs) have been prepared for 13 projects (as of Dec 2025).
The government has identified five priority projects: Ken-Betwa Link, Modified Parbati-Kalisindh-Chambal (PKC) Link, and three sub-links under the Godavari-Cauvery Link.
The Ken-Betwa Link Project (KBLP) is the first and only project under implementation.
The Godavari-Cauvery Link consists of: Godavari (Inchampalli)– Krishna (Nagarjunasagar), Krishna (Nagarjunasagar)–Pennar (Somasila), and Pennar (Somasila)–Cauvery (Grand Anicut). Recent News –
On 19 July 2026, MP Police cleared a 15-day protest against the Ken-Betwa Link Project at Kupi village in Chhatarpur district.
The protest began on 3 July 2026 on the banks of the Barana river near Kupi village in Chhatarpur district, Madhya Pradesh.
Protest leader Amit Bhatnagar, who was on an indefinite hunger strike for 14 days, was hospitalised due to deteriorating health.

The protest, led largely by tribal women, featured symbolic demonstrations including 'jal satyagraha' (water protest), 'chita satyagraha' (funeral pyre protest), and symbolic 'faansi satyagraha' (hanging protest).
Protesters raised the slogan "nyaya do ya maar do" (give justice or kill us), dramatising the "death" of villages facing submergence.
Visuals of women lying on symbolic pyres and placing nooses around their necks drew national attention on social media.
Amit Bhatnagar, founder of Jai Kisan Sangathan, led the agitation and had been on an indefinite hunger strike for 14 days.
Bhatnagar is a social activist who has worked on displacement and rehabilitation issues in Bundelkhand for several years.
Protest leader Divya Ahirwar alleged that Bhatnagar was detained before he could address the media on "corruption of Rs 400 crore" in the project.
Bhatnagar alleged "irregularities" in compensation disbursement, claiming that gram sabha proceedings were fabricated and that ₹8 crore of ₹11 crore was paid to ineligible individuals.
He alleged ₹400 crore corruption in the project, including the inclusion of fake beneficiaries in compensation lists.
Protesters demanded that the rehabilitation package be increased from ₹5 lakh to ₹12.5 lakh per family, and that the cut-off date for eligibility be extended.
Chhatarpur Collector Parth Jaiswal rejected the allegations, stating that 90% of protesters were not project-affected and had come from Panna district with grievances about other projects.
Police justified the action citing safety risks as the protest was staged beneath a bridge and in the river, with water levels rising.
The administration stated that the project is of national importance and will boost irrigation, drinking water supply, and development in Bundelkhand. Other Major River Disputes –
The Cauvery water dispute is one of India's oldest and most contentious inter-State river water conflicts, involving Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala, and Puducherry .
The conflict originated during the British colonial period, with agreements signed in 1892 and 1924 between the Madras Presidency and the princely state of Mysore .
The Supreme Court delivered its landmark judgment on 16 February 2018, modifying the Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal award.
Several inter-State disputes exist over the sharing of waters of the Godavari and Krishna rivers, involving states like Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka, and Maharashtra.
The Polavaram Project on the Godavari has been a source of contention between Andhra Pradesh and neighbouring states.
The Government of India has approved the Revised Cost Estimate of ₹30,436 crore for the Polavaram Project with additional central assistance.
The Narmada Water Dispute involves Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, and Rajasthan.
The dispute was adjudicated by the Narmada Water Disputes Tribunal, which delivered its award in 1979.
The Narmada Bachao Andolan (Save Narmada Movement) was a major social movement opposing the construction of large dams on the Narmada river.
The Ravi-Beas water dispute involves Punjab, Haryana, and Rajasthan.
The dispute arose after the reorganisation of Punjab in 1966, when the waters of the Ravi and Beas rivers had to be shared.
The dispute remains unresolved, with multiple rounds of negotiations and legal proceedings.

topics.title: UK Prime Minsiter
bullets: On 17 July 2026, former Greater Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham was officially confirmed as the new leader of the United Kingdom's governing Labour Party at a special conference in central London.
He will become the UK's seventh Prime Minister in a decade, taking over from Sir Keir Starmer on 20 July 2026.
Burnham was the only candidate in the leadership contest, backed by 379 of the 403 Labour MPs in the House of Commons. UK Parliamentary System –
The United Kingdom operates under a parliamentary system known as the Westminster system, characterised by the fusion of executive and legislative powers.
The Head of Government (Prime Minister) is not directly elected by the public but is the leader of the political party with the most seats in the House of Commons.
The Head of State is the monarch (King Charles III), who performs ceremonial functions including formally appointing the Prime Minister.
The House of Commons is the lower house of the UK Parliament, consisting of 650 Members of Parliament (MPs) elected from single-member constituencies.
MPs are elected using the First-Past-the-Post (FPTP) electoral system, where the candidate with the most votes in each constituency wins the seat.
The Prime Minister must be a sitting MP and command the confidence of the House of Commons to remain in power.
The House of Lords is the upper house of the UK Parliament, consisting of life peers, hereditary peers, and bishops.
Its primary functions are to review and amend legislation proposed by the House of Commons.
The House of Lords cannot veto legislation but can delay it, and its powers have been significantly limited by reforms over the past century.
The monarch (King Charles III) serves as the Head of State and performs ceremonial and constitutional duties.
The monarch's role includes appointing the Prime Minister, giving Royal Assent to legislation, and formally dissolving Parliament before elections.
By constitutional convention, the monarch acts on the advice of the Prime Minister and does not exercise independent political power.
The Prime Minister is the head of the UK government and is appointed by the monarch as the leader of the party that can command a majority in the House of Commons.
The PM holds significant executive powers, including appointing Cabinet ministers, setting government policy, and representing the UK internationally.
The UK can change Prime Ministers without a general election when the ruling party selects a new leader – a phenomenon that has occurred with increasing frequency in recent years.
The Cabinet is the senior decision-making body of the UK government, composed of ministers appointed by the Prime Minister.
Cabinet members are collectively responsible for government policy and must publicly support government decisions or resign.
Major Cabinet positions include the Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance), Home Secretary (interior), and Foreign Secretary (foreign affairs).
General elections are held at least every five years, but the Prime Minister can call an early election with the monarch's approval.
The 2024 general election was held on 4 July 2024, resulting in a landslide victory for the Labour Party.
Labour won 411 of 650 seats, while the Conservatives secured only 121 seats – their lowest ever figure.
Labour Party won the 2024 general election with 411 seats in the House of Commons, a gain of 209 seats compared to the 2019 election.
Sir Keir Starmer became Prime Minister on 5 July 2024, ending 14 years of Conservative rule.
Despite the large parliamentary majority, Labour's vote share was only 33.7% – the lowest of any party to form a majority government since 1830. Andy Burnham –
Andy Burnham (born 7 January 1970) is a 56-year-old politician who served as Mayor of Greater Manchester from 2017 to 2026.
He was previously a Labour MP for Leigh (2001-2017) and served as Health Secretary under Prime Minister Gordon Brown.
He is affectionately known as the "King of the North" for his strong advocacy for northern England.
Burnham returned to Parliament after winning the Makerfield by- election on 18 June 2026 with 24,927 votes.
His victory over the Reform UK candidate by over 9,000 votes convinced many Labour MPs he was the right person to replace Starmer.

The by-election was triggered when the previous MP, Josh Simons, resigned on 14 May 2026. Passage: Allegations of large-scale theft from the donation boxes of the Ram Mandir in Ayodhya generated political and public controversy in 2026. The suspected embezzlement involved individuals entrusted with collecting, transporting and counting offerings made by devotees. Investigators alleged that cash, jewellery and foreign currency were removed from the donation-handling system over an extended period. CCTV footage, changes in the lifestyles of certain suspects and the recovery of cash and valuables reportedly contributed to the investigation. Security deficiencies, including inadequate frisking and ineffective monitoring of surveillance footage, were also identified. Source: The Hindu
